t: Sum of Good Subsequences — Value-Indexed DP
o: Sum the elements of every subsequence whose consecutive elements differ by exactly 1 (singletons count). For [1,2,1] the six good subsequences sum to 14; for [3,4,5] the six sum to 40. Because adjacency depends only on values, we can process the array left to right keeping, per value v, the count c[v] and the sum-of-sums f[v] of good subsequences ending with value v so far. A new element x creates new subsequences by extending those ending at x-1 or x+1, plus the singleton [x].
k: Per value v, maintain (count, sum-of-sums) of good subsequences ending in v; a new element x contributes delta = f[x-1] + f[x+1] + x*(c[x-1] + c[x+1]) + x.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash-Map DP Along the Array
a.i: When element x arrives, every good subsequence ending at x-1 or x+1 can be extended by x (adding x to each of their sums), and [x] itself is new. Add the delta to the global answer and fold it into f[x]/c[x]; subsequences already ending at x persist untouched. Crucially we do NOT extend subsequences ending at x itself, since a difference of 0 is not allowed.
s: Keep dictionaries f (sum of sums) and c (counts) keyed by value.
For each x: delta = f[x-1] + f[x+1] + x*(c[x-1]+c[x+1]) + x (mod 1e9+7).
ans += delta; f[x] += delta; c[x] += c[x-1] + c[x+1] + 1.

c.python:
from collections import defaultdict
class Solution:
    def maximumSum(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        f = defaultdict(int)
        c = defaultdict(int)
        ans = 0
        for x in nums:
            d = (f[x - 1] + f[x + 1] + x * (c[x - 1] + c[x + 1]) + x) % MOD
            ans = (ans + d) % MOD
            f[x] = (f[x] + d) % MOD
            c[x] = (c[x] + c[x - 1] + c[x + 1] + 1) % MOD
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — one constant-time dictionary update per element.
a.sp: O(V) where V is the number of distinct values (bounded by n).

w: The key discipline is adding only the NEW subsequences' contribution to the answer (the delta), while f[x] accumulates the full running total — conflating these double-counts. Verify against both samples: [1,2,1] gives deltas 1, 5, 8 → 14; [3,4,5] gives 3, 11, 26 → 40. Pitfalls: extending same-valued endings (difference 0 is illegal), and overflow of x*c before taking the modulus in C++/Java. Follow-up: count good subsequences by length, or require difference exactly d.
